power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: The sample size was determined before the analyses presented here were planned. Based on Arend and Schäfer (Arend and Schäfer 2019), we estimated that 150 to 200 participants with 6 to 8 measurement occasions would give a power of 80% to detect medium standardized effects (0.20-0.30) at the between-person level and small effects (0.10-0.20) at the within-person level in multilevel models. This calculation does not apply to the improvement classification or the outcome models reported here, which were not powered for a specified effect. We therefore interpret the results by their estimates and credible intervals.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("P > .99", "P = .99", "P = .96", "P = .91", "P = .67"), Sentence = c("PCS improvement had the clearest association with RTW over 3 to 12 months, with RD = 17.6 pp (95% CrI [5.2, 27.1], P > .99).", "WPS improvement (RD = 15.5 pp, 95% CrI [0.7, 25.4], P = .99) and RTW-SE improvement (RD = 14.1 pp, 95% CrI [-0.1, 25.6], P = .96) were also probably associated with a higher probability of RTW.", "WPS improvement (RD = 15.5 pp, 95% CrI [0.7, 25.4], P = .99) and RTW-SE improvement (RD = 14.1 pp, 95% CrI [-0.1, 25.6], P = .96) were also probably associated with a higher probability of RTW.", "Among the baseline scores, WAS had the largest association (RD = 12.2 pp, 95% CrI [-0.5, 23.5], P = .91).", "The largest was for SMBQ physical fatigue improvement in months 4-6, -0.1 days (95% CrI [-22.9, 1.3], P = .67)." )), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: Purpose: Common mental disorders (CMDs), including depression, anxiety, and adjustment disorders, are leading causes of long-term sickness absence (SA) and work disability in highincome countries.
Despite the significant burden, evidence-based interventions to support return to work (RTW) remain limited.

This study aimed to investigate the predictive role of selected modifiable psychological factors on RTW among individuals on sick leave for CMDs, with particular emphasis on temporal dynamics during the early phase of the RTW process.

Methods: A longitudinal observational study of 165 participants on sick leave for CMDs was conducted with bi-weekly self-reported questionnaire measurements for 3 months and quarterly follow-ups for 12 months.
Outcomes were self-reported work status (working to the full extent of one's employment, RTW) and registry-based net SA days (NSAD) in each quarter.

Analyses included robust linear mixed models to classify improvement in seven focal predictors during the first three months, Bayesian logistic regression with a regularizing horseshoe prior for the probability of RTW, and ordered beta regression for NSAD.
All models were adjusted for the baseline values of all focal predictors and for covariates.

Results: Over 3 to 12 months, improvement in perceived competence was associated with a higher probability of RTW, with a risk difference (RD) of 17.6 percentage points (95% credible interval, CrI [5.2, 27.1]).
Improvement in workplace phobia (RD = 15.5, 95% CrI [0.7, 25.4]) and RTW self-efficacy (RTW-SE, RD = 14.1, 95% CrI [-0.1, 25.6]) showed similar differences.
At 3 months, RTW-SE improvement was associated with RD = 21.5 (95% CrI [0.1, 32.8]).
No focal predictor was associated with NSAD in any quarter.
Early improvement in work-related psychological factors was associated with later work status, but not with compensated sickness absence.
Whether strengthening these factors can support RTW is a question for further study.

Common mental disorders (CMDs), including depression, anxiety, and adjustment disorders, are leading contributors to work disability worldwide, placing a substantial burden on individuals, employers, and healthcare systems (World Health Organization 2022; OECD 2023).

text.text: In Sweden, CMDs represent the most prevalent diagnostic group associated with long-term sick leave, particularly among women and younger individuals (Försäkringskassan (Swedish Social Insurance Agency) 2024).

text.text: Returning to work (RTW) following sickness absence (SA) related to CMDs is a complex process, influenced by both individual and contextual factors (Nieuwenhuijsen et al. 2006; Etuknwa et al. 2019; Duchemin and Hocine 2020).

text.text: Previous studies have identified several predictors of RTW for individuals with CMDs, including younger age, higher education, fewer prior sickness absences, lower symptom severity, greater self-efficacy, positive RTW expectations, better sleep quality, and support from supervisors and colleagues (de Vries et al. 2018; Etuknwa et al. 2019; Fisker et al. 2022; Villotti et al. 2024).

text.text: Modifiable psychosocial factors are of particular interest as potential targets for intervention (Villotti et al. 2024).
text.formatted: Modifiable psychosocial factors are of particular interest as potential targets for intervention <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Villotti et al. 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Among these, RTW self-efficacy, defined as an individual's belief in their ability to resume and manage work despite mental health challenges (Lagerveld et al. 2010), has emerged as a key predictor of successful RTW (Volker et al. 2015; Nigatu et al. 2017).
text.formatted: Among these, RTW self-efficacy, defined as an individual's belief in their ability to resume and manage work despite mental health challenges <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Lagerveld et al. 2010)</ref>, has emerged as a key predictor of successful RTW <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Volker et al. 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Nigatu et al. 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Research indicates that stable or increasing self-efficacy over time is associated with earlier RTW (Lagerveld et al. 2017; Horn et al. 2022); however, current evidence is based on measurement intervals usually spaced 3 months apart.
text.formatted: Research indicates that stable or increasing self-efficacy over time is associated with earlier RTW <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Lagerveld et al. 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Horn et al. 2022</ref>); however, current evidence is based on measurement intervals usually spaced 3 months apart.

text.text: To date, no studies have incorporated more frequent assessments during the critical early period (0-3 months) post-baseline.
Predictors of RTW may also vary depending on the duration of the SA episode.

For instance, factors that are influential early in the absence period (< 3 months) may differ from those relevant in later phases, yet few studies have examined this potential temporal variation (Fisker et al. 2022).
text.formatted: For instance, factors that are influential early in the absence period (< 3 months) may differ from those relevant in later phases, yet few studies have examined this potential temporal variation <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Fisker et al. 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, it remains unclear whether predictors maintain a consistent influence throughout the RTW process or if their predictive value changes over time.
Accurately capturing RTW and SA outcomes presents further methodological challenges.

Sick leave may vary in duration, frequency, extent (part-or full-time), and recurrence with different metrics used across studies, complicating comparability (Hensing et al. 1998; Duchemin and Hocine 2020).
text.formatted: Sick leave may vary in duration, frequency, extent (part-or full-time), and recurrence with different metrics used across studies, complicating comparability <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Hensing et al. 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Duchemin and Hocine 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Sole reliance on metrics such as counting days based on registry data may obscure the complexity of the RTW process.
Registry data needs to comply with regulations in the country of origin, which may make comparisons between countries difficult.

Also, variables predicting registry data could be more closely related to system level and health care factors, such as policies and physician guidelines, that are difficult to quantify and include in a statistical model.
Focusing on individual level factors only is less challenging but will likely be limited in explaining variation in registry data.
There are also important methodological concerns in the field.

One relates to the treatment of data, where non-categorical variables are most often treated as interval level data in statistical models, even if a variable is clearly ordinal in nature, such as a single item measure.
This may influence inference significantly (Liddell and Kruschke 2018).
text.formatted: This may influence inference significantly <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Liddell and Kruschke 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Multi-item ordinal sum scores have less clear statistical properties, but visualizing the distribution of the data is important to choose a correct statistical model, rather than just assuming data to be normally distributed.
Number of sick days is a count variable with a lower bound, which also has a known upper bound since the time span is known and thus the maximum number of days possible.
In the methods section, we will describe a statistical model that handles bounded data properly.
Another important aspect is psychometric quality of measures used.

A paradigm shift is ongoing in psychometrics, moving from rule-of-thumb model fit cutoffs that are known to be inappropriate for most analyses to simulation-based cutoffs (Goretzko et al. 2024; Johansson 2025).
text.formatted: A paradigm shift is ongoing in psychometrics, moving from rule-of-thumb model fit cutoffs that are known to be inappropriate for most analyses to simulation-based cutoffs <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Goretzko et al. 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Johansson 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This calls for re-analyses of old scales, no matter which psychometric method has been applied previously, to evaluate and likely modify measures according to findings from correctly applied methods.

As a final methodological note, we want to mention the "Table 2 fallacy" (Westreich and Greenland 2013; Bandoli et al. 2018), which briefly stated is related to the interpretation of regression coefficients.

text.text: Since a statistical model is usually constructed to evaluate the total effects of a focal predictor (such as a treatment) on the outcome (for instance RTW), it does not follow that the coefficients of other predictor variables can be interpreted as total effects as well.

This is especially important to consider if one's statistical model uses the hazard ratio or Odd's ratio, since these estimands are non-collapsible and will change depending on the set of covariates included in the model (Cummings 2009; Dumas and Stensrud 2025; Colnet et al. 2025).

text.text: To inform the development of effective RTW interventions, a deeper understanding of how modifiable psychosocial predictors function and evolve over time is essential.

In this exploratory longitudinal observational study, we aim to investigate the role of selected modifiable psychological factors in explaining RTW among individuals on sick leave for CMDs, with a particular focus on temporal dynamics during the early phase of the RTW process.
We used two outcomes that describe different aspects of recovery.

Self-reported work status describes whether participants were working to the full extent of their employment at each assessment, and registered net sickness absence days (NSAD) describe the amount of compensated sickness absence in each quarter of the year after inclusion.
The study was designed as a longitudinal observational study and is reported in accordance with
The Strengthening the Reporting of Observational studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines.
The Swedish Ethical Review Authority approved the study protocol (Dnr:2021-05022).
Participants were recruited between April 2022 and February 2023 via advertisements in social media and posters displayed at primary healthcare centers in Region Stockholm, Sweden.
The advertisements contained a link to a secure website with information about the study and how to register to participate.
Following registration, participants were contacted by phone for an interview where inclusion criteria were checked to confirm their eligibility.
At the interview, participants reported the diagnosis stated on their medical certificate as the reason for their sick leave, and checked the certificate when needed.
The certificates were not collected, so diagnostic eligibility was based on self-report.
Self-reported data were collected using the digital research platform BASS from the eHealth Core Facility at Karolinska Institutet.
Written informed consent was obtained from all participants.
To promote adherence to the measurement protocol, participants were offered the option of receiving an incentive at each quarterly assessment point.
They could choose between a cinema voucher or lottery tickets as a form of compensation.
The inclusion criteria were: age 18-60 and currently (for a duration of less than six weeks) on full-or part-time SA due to a common mental disorder (CMD).

The accepted diagnoses according to the criteria of the ICD-10 (World Health Organization 2019) were: F32 depressive episode; F33 recurrent depressive disorder; F34 persistent mood [affective] disorders; F38 other mood [affective] disorders; F39 unspecified mood [affective] disorder; F41 other anxiety disorders; F43 adjustment disorders and reactions to severe stress; and F48 other neurotic disorders.
All forms of comorbidities, both physical and psychological, were accepted, as well as all kinds of medication.
The follow-up measurements require a good understanding of written Swedish, participants who did not meet this inclusion criteria were thus excluded.
The sample size was determined before the analyses presented here were planned.

Based on Arend and Schäfer (Arend and Schäfer 2019), we estimated that 150 to 200 participants with 6 to 8 measurement occasions would give a power of 80% to detect medium standardized effects (0.20-0.30) at the between-person level and small effects (0.10-0.20) at the within-person level in multilevel models.
This calculation does not apply to the improvement classification or the outcome models reported here, which were not powered for a specified effect.
We therefore interpret the results by their estimates and credible intervals.
Demographic data and background variables (such as age, gender, type of work, level of education, etc.) were collected at enrollment.
Assessments were conducted weekly during the first 10 weeks and then quarterly until one year after inclusion.
Weekly assessments alternated between health and work measures on a biweekly basis.
Register data were obtained from the Swedish Social Insurance Agency database MiDAS (Micro-Data for Analysis of the Social Insurance System) 12 months prior to inclusion to 12 months after inclusion.
All residents in Sweden with income from work, unemployment, or parental leave benefits can receive SA benefits if their work capacity is reduced due to disease or injury.
For employees, the employer pays SA benefits for the first 13 days of a SA period after the first qualifying day.
A medical certificate is required from day eight.
After the 14th day, the Social Insurance Agency pays the benefits, covering approximately 80% of lost income up to a certain level.
All residents aged 19-64 years with a long-term or permanently reduced work capacity due to disease or injury can be granted disability pension (DP).
Both SA and DP may be granted full-or part-time (25%, 50%, 75%) of ordinary working hours.
Data also included main diagnosis (according to ICDclassification) from the sickness certification granted.
Two outcomes were included.

First, self-reported work status, for which participants were asked about their current level of work activity at each assessment, with response options of 0, 25, 50, 75, and 100 percent of their own employment.
The variable was dichotomized into working to the full extent of one's employment (100%) or less.
For participants employed part-time, 100% thus means working the full extent of that employment.
Contracted hours were not recorded.
In the following, RTW refers to working to the full extent of one's employment at an assessment.
The outcome describes work status at each assessment and does not show when a participant first returned to work or whether the return was sustained.
Second, net sickness absence days (NSAD), for which we calculated SA/DP net days; e.g., two days of part-time absence for 50% were summed to one net day.
NSAD was calculated for each quarter after enrollment (months 1-3, 4-6, 7-9 and 10-12), each with a maximum of 90 days, and each quarter was used as the outcome in separate statistical models.
All models included the same covariates, all measured at or before enrollment.

They included demographic variables, ongoing treatments, pain, general health, and single-item assessments of sleep quality, employer facilitation of workplace adjustments (EFWA), the Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2, (Kroenke et al. 2003)), and the Demands, Control and Social Support Questionnaire (DCSQ, (Sanne et al. 2005)).

text.text: Sleep quality and EFWA were assessed using single questionnaire items with 7 and 11 ordered response categories, respectively.
While the sleep quality item provided descriptive labels for all response categories, the EFWA item included labels only at the endpoints.
The distribution of responses for the sleep quality item was approximately normal.
In contrast, the EFWA response distribution was very irregular, with the most frequently selected categories being 1 (30%), 5 (13%), and 10 (11%).
This distribution posed challenges for statistical modeling.
To address this, the EFWA responses were collapsed into three ordered categories: 0-3 (53% of responses), 4-7 (24%), and 8-10 (22%).
PHQ-2 contains two items, each with four ordered response categories scored from 0-3, and was dichotomized using ordinal sum score ≥ 3 as a cutoff for risk indication (Manea et al. 2016).

text.text: Two register-based variables described sickness absence during the 12 months before inclusion: any sickness absence (yes/no) and the number of net sickness absence days (log-transformed) (Lorenz et al. 2017).

text.text: All covariates and their coding are listed in the Additional materials.
Our focal predictors consisted of six multi-item questionnaires and one single-item measure, assessed biweekly from enrollment to 3 months after enrollment.

We use the term "focal predictor" to clarify that statistical models and post-modeling effect estimations are designed to investigate the effect of the focal variables on the outcome (Arel-Bundock et al. 2024; Rohrer and Arel-Bundock 2025), to avoid the "factors associated with" issue if we were to interpret model coefficients of all variables included in the model (Lewer et al. 2025).

text.text: All multi-item measurement scales were subject to psychometric analysis using Rasch measurement theory (Rasch 1960), assessing the basic psychometric criteria of unidimensionality (for each subscale in multidimensional scales), local independence of items, ordered response categories, and invariance (Christensen et al. 2021).

text.text: The retained items, response categories, score ranges and measurement occasions for each scale are listed in the Additional materials.
Repeated measurements of the focal predictors were not imputed.
The robust growth models (see below) used all available observations, and each participant's baseline value was the mean of their available scores at the first two assessments.
Missing data among the baseline covariates were limited to five binary treatment variables (2 to 7 missing values each), and 15 participants (9%) lacked at least one.
Missing covariates and work status were handled using multiple imputation with chained equations, as implemented in the R package ´mice´ (van Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn 2011).
For RTW, data were imputed in wide format with one row per participant, so that work status at all ten assessments entered the imputation model as separate variables.
The treatment covariates and work status were imputed by logistic regression, with predictors selected by a minimum correlation of 0.1.

Twenty datasets were imputed, which meets the recommendation of at least as many imputations as the percentage of incomplete cases (White et al. 2011), using 50 iterations and visually inspected for convergence.
text.formatted: Twenty datasets were imputed, which meets the recommendation of at least as many imputations as the percentage of incomplete cases <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(White et al. 2011)</ref>, using 50 iterations and visually inspected for convergence.

text.text: Imputed work statuses were retained in both the cross-sectional and the longitudinal models, since work status at other assessments, including those before 3 months, informs the imputed values and is not part of the analysis models.
For NSAD, only the treatment covariates were imputed, with the NSAD outcomes as predictors.
All statistical models were fitted to each of the 20 datasets separately.
Since we used Bayesian outcome models, results were pooled by combining the posterior draws from all submodels.
The RTW analyses thus included all 165 participants, and the NSAD analyses the 141 with registered sickness absence (see Results).
As a sensitivity analysis, all models were also fitted to complete cases, the 150 participants with complete covariate data.

The cross-sectional RTW models then included those with an observed work status at each time point (147 at 3 months, 140 at 6 months, 135 at 12 months), the longitudinal model all observed assessments at 3 to 12 months (148 participants, 560 observations), and the NSAD models 127 participants.
These analyses assume that missingness does not depend on the outcome given the variables in the model.
Complete-case results are reported in the Additional materials.

Each focal predictor was used in two ways: as a baseline measurement using the mean of the two first assessments and as a dichotomous variable indicating either participant improvement or lack of improvement during the first three months.
For each of the focal predictors, a robust linear mixed model (LMM) with random slopes and intercepts was fitted using the R package `robustlmm` (Koller 2016), with time in weeks since inclusion.
text.formatted: For each of the focal predictors, a robust linear mixed model (LMM) with random slopes and intercepts was fitted using the R package `robustlmm` <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Koller 2016)</ref>, with time in weeks since inclusion.

text.text: The models used the assessments from enrollment to 3 months, with the mean of the first two assessments as the first time point.
The robust method for this unconditional growth model was chosen after checking non-robust models and finding issues with outliers.
Improvement was classified from each participant's full estimated slope, that is, the fixed slope plus the participant's random deviation.

Participants whose slope exceeded half the standard deviation (SD) of the random slopes in the favourable direction (an increase for RTW-SE, PCS and WAS, a decrease for WPS, SMBQ and GAD-4) were coded as 1 for "improved", and the others as 0 for "not improved".

The threshold is thus defined relative to the model-estimated variation in slopes between participants, which is in the same unit as the classified quantity and is not inflated by residual measurement error.
R code and a worked example are given in the Additional materials.
The improvement categories were treated as fixed in the outcome models, so the reported intervals are conditional on the classification and do not include its uncertainty.

Results from all robust LMMs and slope categorizations are summarized in Table 2, which also gives the threshold in score units and includes a heterogeneity ratio, calculated as the SD of the random slopes divided by the absolute fixed slope (Vuorre et al. 2024) to describe the relative variation in change over time, as well as the ICC.

We chose to model the probability of RTW using both cross-sectional and longitudinal models.
Cross-sectional models used data from 3, 6, and 12 months.
The 3-month assessment is the last point of the period in which improvement was classified, so associations with RTW at 3 months are concurrent with improvement.
Associations at 6 and 12 months are prospective but may reflect work resumed during the improvement period.
Since the categorical variable "RTW-SE improved" had quasi-separation at one time point, a regularizing model was needed.
The crosssectional analyses were modeled with Bayesian logistic regression with a regularized horseshoe prior (Piironen and Vehtari 2017) using the R package `brms` (Bürkner 2021).

text.text: The regularizing horseshoe prior imposes shrinkage towards zero on predictor coefficients, except in cases where a predictor exerts a substantial influence on the outcome.
In such instances, the prior has little impact.
For all focal predictors in all models, we report posterior medians with 95% equal-tailed credible intervals (CrI).
Equal-tailed intervals were used since they remain valid when coefficients are transformed into odds ratios (OR) or probabilities.
We also report P, the posterior probability that an association is in the expected direction (a higher probability of RTW, or fewer NSAD).
P is not a frequentist p-value.

It is the probability, given the data and the model, that the association has the expected direction, so values close to 1 indicate strong support for that direction and values close to .5 indicate no support for either direction.

We report the average probability of RTW at each assessment, and for each focal predictor the average difference in the probability of RTW (risk difference, RD), in percentage points (pp), over the 3 to 12 month period and at each assessment.

The model has no interaction between the focal predictor and time, so the conditional OR is constant over time, while the difference in probability varies because the probability of RTW changes over time.

Each improvement model included the improvement indicator for one focal predictor together with the baseline values of all seven focal predictors and the covariates, so that each improvement association is adjusted for starting level.
Improvement in the other focal predictors was not included, since it occurred during the same period as the focal improvement and is not a baseline confounder.

For the same reason, the baseline models included the baseline values of all seven focal predictors and the covariates but no improvement indicators, since improvement may lie on the path from baseline status to the outcome.
The two model sets thus address separate questions: whether status at entry is associated with later work outcomes, and whether early improvement is associated with them beyond status at entry.

text.text: In this exploratory longitudinal observational study, we investigated modifiable psychological variables as predictors for RTW after sickness absence due to CMD, focusing on temporal dynamics of different variables during the early phase of the SA episode.
Two different outcomes were evaluated: self-reported RTW and net sickness absence days (NSAD).
The RTW analyses showed that work-related psychological factors had the clearest associations with RTW.

In the cross-sectional models, a more favourable baseline RTW-SE score and RTW-SE improvement were associated with RTW at 3 months, which is concurrent with the period in which improvement was classified.

At 6 and 12 months, RTW-SE improvement at 6 months and PCS improvement at 12 months were probably positively associated with RTW, with intervals that included zero, while baseline RTW-SE showed no association.
These later associations are prospective but may reflect work resumed during the improvement period.

In the longitudinal models of RTW at 3 to 12 months, improvement in PCS, WPS and RTW-SE was associated with a higher probability of RTW, with RDs of 14 to 18 pp over the period, and among the baseline scores WAS had the largest association.
The intervals were wide, so the size of these associations is uncertain.
The 3-month RTW-SE association in particular rests on few participants without improvement who had returned to work.
In contrast, no focal predictor was associated with NSAD in any quarter after the improvement period, and no baseline score was associated with NSAD in months 1-3.

Improvement and baseline scores describe different contrasts, improved versus not improved and the 75th versus the 25th percentile of the baseline score, and their relative size does not show which provides better predictions.
Information on improvement is also available three months later than the baseline assessment.
We therefore do not interpret these results as a comparison of predictive performance.
The associations between early improvement and work status at 6 to 12 months are exploratory findings that may be of prognostic relevance.
The unconditional growth models for each of the seven focal predictor variables also led to some interesting findings.
We summarized results in Table 2, where notable levels of both heterogeneity and ICC are shown.

This highlights the importance of using random intercepts and slopes to correctly model heterogeneity.
The heterogeneity ratio (H-ratio) is a relatively new metric that, to our knowledge, has not been previously reported in studies in this field.

By using the average of the first two measurements our baseline measures should also be robust.

In our data, improvement during the first three months was associated with later work status beyond status at entry, but this does not show that improvement is a better predictor than baseline status.
In planning the study, focal predictor variables were selected to represent two distinct domains: symptomatology and work-related psychological factors.
Work-related psychological factors (RTW-SE, WPS and PCS) had the clearest associations with RTW, whereas the symptom measures did not.
Work-related factors have also been associated with sickness absence in previous research (Fisker et al. 2022; Frantz et al. 2025).

text.text: These findings further underscore the importance of emphasizing work-oriented processes in RTW interventions.
Most participants exhibited improvements in symptom severity during the initial three-month period compared to baseline.
However, neither improvement nor baseline levels of physical fatigue, cognitive weariness or worry had clear associations with RTW or NSAD in the adjusted analyses.

Weak associations with these outcomes do not establish low value for other clinical purposes, such as assessing symptoms or treatment needs, and any suggestion to reduce questionnaire burden applies to RTW research only.

It is important to distinguish between modifiable predictors, such as psychosocial factors, and non-modifiable variables, including sociodemographic characteristics, which remain We chose to include two distinct outcome measures: one based on participants' self-reported work participation, dichotomized into working to the full extent of one's employment or less, and another derived from registry data indicating the number of days compensated by the sickness insurance system.
The findings differed between the two outcomes.
Early improvement and baseline status were associated with working to the full extent of one's employment, but not with the amount of compensated absence later in the year.
Notably, a portion of the sample had no recorded sickness benefit days, possibly due to ending their sick leave within the initial 15 days or not meeting eligibility criteria for compensation.
These participants were excluded from the NSAD analyses, so those results may not apply to people whose absence ended before compensation began.
The excluded group differed from the others mainly in age, and was not more often working at 3 months, so an early end to sick leave does not seem to explain most of the missing register data.
The dichotomized RTW variable is unable to reflect gradients of increased work participation, which may be better reflected in the NSAD variable.
This highlights the importance of employing a broader set of measurement tools to capture diverse trajectories within the population.

While self-reported data may offer more nuanced insights into individual-level processes, registry data are influenced by external factors such as the physician's assessment and certification, as well as the case officer's evaluation of the medical certificate and its qualification for sickness benefit.
The combination of highfrequency measurements and self-reported data enabled the identification of intermittent patterns in sickness absence, revealing both "on" and "off" statuses over time.
While this provides valuable insight into the temporal dynamics of absence, it also presents methodological challenges related to data interpretation and classification.
Net sickness absence days (NSAD) is a bounded variable, with lower and upper limits given by the observation period.
In our data, many participants were at the lower bound and some at the upper bound in each quarter.

Ordered beta regression (Kubinec 2023) accommodates values at both bounds, and posterior predictive checks were used to assess how well the models reproduced the shares at both bounds and the distribution between them (Additional materials).

text.text: Two different types of data were used to assess RTW.
The method section provides a thorough description of the statistical analyses used and the reasons for each decision.
Together with the model specifications provided in the Additional materials, this increases transparency and the possibility of replication in future studies.
Other researchers can both criticize and perhaps learn from our chosen methods.

While we do not assert that the assumptions for interpreting results from g-computation as causal effects are fulfilled, the method allows us to present results in an easily interpretable way on the scale of the outcome variable (probability of RTW and number of days).
This method also reduces risk of the "Table 2 fallacy" (Westreich and Greenland 2013).
text.formatted: This method also reduces risk of the "Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> fallacy" <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Westreich and Greenland 2013)</ref>.

text.text: It is important to note that while we are interested in causal relationships between predictor and outcome variables, our non-randomized uncontrolled data does not allow us to make strong causal claims.
In particular, the associations do not show that producing improvement in a focal predictor would increase work participation.

The chosen analysis strategy was exploratory rather than theory driven, as we included a large number of predictor variables and used data-driven methods to examine the associations between multiple variables and the outcomes.

A stronger causal inference methodology would include drawing causal diagrams, often referred to as directed acyclical graphs (DAGs, (Shrier and Platt 2008; Rohrer 2018), which illustrate á priori assumptions about causal relationships between variables used to determine appropriate adjustment sets for each pair of outcome and focal predictor.
text.formatted: A stronger causal inference methodology would include drawing causal diagrams, often referred to as directed acyclical graphs (DAGs, <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Shrier and Platt 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Rohrer 2018)</ref>, which illustrate á priori assumptions about causal relationships between variables used to determine appropriate adjustment sets for each pair of outcome and focal predictor.

text.text: Our question concerned being at work at each assessment, for which models of work status are appropriate.
Time-to-event models address the timing of transitions into or out of work, which is a different question.
Models for recurrent events, for example time-to-event models that can handle multiple event occurrences with different durations (Amorim and Cai 2015), could be used to study such transitions.
text.formatted: Models for recurrent events, for example time-to-event models that can handle multiple event occurrences with different durations <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Amorim and Cai 2015)</ref>, could be used to study such transitions.

text.text: Including only baseline measurements of the focal predictor variables rather than using them as time-varying covariates limits the possibility of understanding co-variation between variables across time.

The large heterogeneity of change in the focal predictor variables between individuals during the first 3 months of the study was perhaps coarsely captured by the "improved" or "not improved" dichotomous variable created.
Further investigation of this heterogeneity and how it relates to outcomes such as RTW is warranted.

A statistical modeling method that could have been used is to allow predictor variables to vary across time rather than using only the baseline measurements and the categories (improved/not improved), or the categorization could have used more than two levels.
We did not conduct any sensitivity analyses regarding the amount of change occurring during shorter time spans.

The improvement categories were treated as fixed in the outcome models, so the reported intervals do not include the uncertainty in the classification and are likely too narrow, and misclassification near the threshold would tend to attenuate the associations.
The baseline value and the estimated slope share the first time point.
Improvement was classified during the first three months, so associations with RTW at 3 months cannot establish whether improvement preceded work resumption or followed it.
Missing covariates and work status were handled with multiple imputation, which assumes that missingness depends only on observed variables.
Complete-case analyses gave similar but somewhat smaller estimates for RTW and similar estimates for NSAD.
As previously noted, for 13 participants the diagnosis stated in the sickness certificate was not one of the accepted diagnoses for inclusion.
This discrepancy may be due to the nature of the registry data only reporting the initial main diagnosis.
Secondary diagnoses in the certificates are not shown in register data.
Since diagnostic eligibility was based on self-report and the certificates were not collected, we cannot rule out that some participants did not have an eligible diagnosis.

These results apply to people with CMD who were recruited within six weeks of the start of sick leave and followed for 12 months, and may not apply to people already on long-term sick leave when first assessed.
Participants were self-selected through advertisements and were treated in different settings, mainly primary care, which may limit generalizability to other recruitment routes and settings.
The results are relevant for Sweden and other countries with similar health care and insurance systems.
Only small proportions of the included participants were male, which may limit the generalizability to men.
The reported analyses could inform future studies in terms of power analysis and setting priors in Bayesian statistical models.

Improvement in work-related psychological factors during the first three months was associated with a higher probability of working to the full extent of one's employment during the following year, while symptom measures did not show a significant relationship with RTW.
None of the focal predictors was associated with compensated sickness absence days.
Our findings suggest that interventions aiming to support RTW should target work-related factors and monitor their development, especially during the early phase of sick-leave.
Whether strengthening these factors can support RTW is a question for further study.

The RTW process is inherently dynamic, with both internal and external conditions subject to change.
Consequently, baseline measurements may lose relevance as time progresses.
Repeated assessments are therefore essential to accurately capture the evolving nature of the RTW trajectory and to inform timely and individualized interventions.

In this study, average NSAD decreased from about 43 days in months 1-3 to 15 days in months 10-12, but none of the focal predictors was associated with NSAD in any quarter.The lack of associations with NSAD suggests that the individual-level psychological factors studied here explain little of the variation in compensated sickness absence.
A systemic approach is required to disentangle the complex interplay of factors influencing the individual RTW process.

Contextual variables, such as the structure of the insurance system, certification practices, workplace conditions, and broader socio-environmental influences, are essential for a comprehensive understanding of RTW trajectories.
Nevertheless, to inform the development of targeted treatment strategies, it is equally important to identify and understand modifiable psychosocial factors at the individual level.
